newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/FOMC- Will they go? Do we care?.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/FOMC- Will they go? Do we care?.

text.p: For weeks the debate has raged on Wall Street, where interest rates are an obsession.
For weeks economists have scrutinized employment and production figures and analysts have pored over the words of Federal Reserve officials for a clue to the decision.
On Tuesday, the market finally learns the answer to the one question on everyone's mind: Will they or won't they?
"They" refers, of course, to the Federal Reserve and the question is whether or not the Fed will increase interest rates this week in an effort to forestall inflation.

In the latest Reuters poll, conducted Thursday, 16 of 30 economists surveyed said the Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee (FOMC) would raise interest rates by one-fourth of a percentage point (25 basis points) at its September 24 meeting.
Thirteen economists said the Fed would leave rates unchanged and one predicted a hike of half a percentage point.
Yet, even with attention so squarely fixed upon and opinion so divided over this Fed meeting, only lately has a second question come to be addressed, namely: What difference does it make?

Analysts generally expect little stock market fallout in the event of a modest increase in the federal funds rate, currently targeted at 5.25 percent, because the market has acted to discount such a move.
"If the Fed raises by 25 basis points, that's already priced in the market," said Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
Likewise, a Fed vote to leave rates unchanged is only expected to provide a short-lived, modest boost.

"If there's no change, I think there will be a mild celebration," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "But people may construe the decision as deferring to political sensibilities because the Presidential debate will only be about a week away."
Indeed, of the 13 respondents to the Reuter poll who predicted no rise in rates, seven forecast a Fed tightening in late November, just after the U.S. Presidential elections.

On the surface, the outlook would seem to present a problem for the stock market, which clearly favors lower rates. However, the jitters about the fallout of a Fed move appear tamer than in the recent past.

One reason is that the market is devoid of the speculative fervor that fueled a fierce small-cap rally early in the year and, by most indicators, smaller-cap stocks have yet to recoup their losses from the July correction.
Another is that recent data have delivered mixed signals about the state of the economy and the spectre of inflation.
Despite a steep decline in the nation's unemployment rate and robust wage growth, companies have shown no ability to translate higher labor costs into price increases.
Until a clearer sign emerges on the inflation front, analysts do not really expect Tuesday's outcome to settle anything at all.
"I don't want to make the (FOMC meeting on the) 24th the be-all and end-all," Wachtel said, "because everybody realizes this is a work in progress."
